To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children with CIs exhibit differences in their productions of sibilant frication relative to NH children.
children with CIs produce less contrast between /s/- and /∫/, and this is associated with a shallower trajectory of the peak frequency and a shallower trajectory for the amplitude drop.

(1) children with cochlear (CI) implants produced less acoustic contrast than children with normal hearing (CH) for word-initial sibilant frications; (2) children with CIs had more asymmetric and shallow spectral trajectories than CH for sibilant-fricative productions; and (3) the intelligibility of children with CIs’ productions was sensitive to the place-of-articulation of the initial frication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acoustic properties of word-initial sibilant frication and how they affect the intelligibility of single-word productions by 4- to 7-year-old children with CIs.
the acoustic and perceptual properties of fricatives in children with CIs.
how children with CIs produce and perceive fricative consonants and how these differences affect the intelligibility of word-level productions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children with CIs produce less subphonemic contrast in their sibilant frications than do NH children, and this difference affects the intelligibility of their productions.

children with CIs are less able to produce the subphonemic acoustic contrasts that differentiate sibilant fricates, and that these differences in subphoneme acoustic contrast are related to the intelligibility of their sibilant-initial word productions.

children with CIs exhibit differential production abilities and subphonemic acoustic contrasts for sibilant initial consonants that affect word-level intelligibility, but the differences are smaller in magnitude than those observed in previous studies that used only static acoustic properties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children with CIs exhibit reduced acoustic contrast between /∫/ and /s/, and that this reduced contrast is reflected in the intelligibility of word-level productions.

children with CIs are able to learn the subphonemic acoustic features of fricative production, but their ability to produce them with the same degree of contrast as their NH peers is still developing.

the subphonemic acoustic contrasts between /s/–/∫/ in the productions of children with CIs are less robust than in their peers with NH, which in turn may contribute to reduced intelligibility of s-initial words.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children with CIs may be producing the fricative /∫/ with a reduced sibilant component, and this reduced sibilance may be contributing to the increased intelligibility of /∫/-words.
the intelligibility of word-level productions by children with CI is sensitive to the dynamic aspects of the subphonemic acoustic features of sibilant frications.
the subphonemic acoustic differences between sibilants produced by children with CI and their peers with normal-hearing are not just about place of articulation.
